rv.q: An American in Paris is a lightfooted antidote to gloom, filled with lovers of Chagall-like airiness. Even the scene-changing involves ballet – bentwood chairs twirled overhead like dancing partners. Christopher Wheeldon, director and choreographer, has done a fabulous job.
The entire edifice is so beautifully engineered that there isn't a weak spot or a dull moment.
It’s a richly satisfying show, delivered with heart and flair.
This lavish musical is such a tonic it should be available on prescription.
Christopher Wheeldon's An American in Paris is a whirl of colour and imagery, a fantasy Paris rooted to a specific historical moment.
Let’s celebrate the repeatedly inventive staging of director/choreographer Christopher Wheeldon and his designer Bob Crowley.
When dance predominates, especially in the pair's most eloquently intimate scenes, this is a glorious experience.
The result is a sophisticated-looking musical that radiates good taste and good intentions, but doesn’t really catch fire.
As grand escapism, An American in Paris – a Broadway adaptation of a Hollywood movie-musical – is superb, despite its attempts to introduce a little darkness to the 1951 original.

Well George Gershwin for one, since even a lovelorn song such as But Not For Me is sheer delight in this glorious musical reclamation. One of the last great MGM musicals, the 1951 film was a vehicle as much for Gene Kelly’s choreographic ambitions as Gershwin’s score.

cn.t: Wheeldon's lavish adaptation dazzles with gorgeous choreography, sumptuous design, and Gershwin's glorious score, though critics note the plot remains thin. Most hail it as an exhilarating, graceful tonic that adds postwar shadows to MGM sunshine.
